title.narrative: Women-Adapt: Enhancing the climate change adaptive capacity of smallholder farmer communities in the Poro Region, focusing on vulnerable women and youth

description.narrative:
1. The project will strengthen adaptive capacities and enhance the livelihoods’ resilience of women smallholder farmer communities by disseminating a ‘package’ of integrated, gender-transformative solutions identified on the basis of the possible intervention priorities along with strategic approaches described in the pre feasibility study[1] [https://wfp.sharepoint.com/sites/GCFCotedIvoire/Shared%20Documents/General/Concept%20Note%20development/Concept%20Note%20&%20attachments/4.%20Fourth%20submission%20to%20the%20GCF%20(December%202021)/GCF%20SAP-concept-note_Cote%20d'Ivoire_WFP_Revised_November2021_final.docx#_ftn1]. It is structured under three intertwined components that tackle the main climate change hazards affecting Poro Region (droughts, interannual rainfall variability and heavy floods and winds) and the above-mentioned adaptation barriers. The gender-transformative nature of this project revolves around the highly significant participation, awareness, strengthening of skills, leadership and financial capacities of women for all project activities from community to household levels. Households headed by women and women-led FOs will be involved in climate empowerment actions key to the project scope:
· Awareness-raising about climate change hazards and impacts to local livelihoods
· Participatory mapping of selected climate-resilient measures to address adaptation barriers
· Training and capacity-building of adapted livelihoods options, climate risk products and services for small-scale food production,
· Implementation and dissemination of a set of integrated adaptive measures including nature-based solutions and climate-risk management tools (C1 and C2)
· Empowerment of FOs through financial literacy, organizational management, access to savings and loans (C3)
· Linkages with markets and improved sales of staple crops and vegetables while fostering climate-proofing investments (C3)
2. The project seeks to roll out a participatory process calling for evidence-based and results-driven interventions. These will demonstrate that, when key root causes of inequalities are addressed, both men and women can bring about positive change in their communities. The project will create an enabling environment to bring to the front of the discussions with local stakeholders the importance of ensuring women have equal access to improved agricultural inputs and means of production. Women are usually given access to less productive marginal lands to carry out their crop production. To address this inequality, the project will engage men and youth in land-reclamation and land-restorations and erosion control activities. Women, like men, will be given an opportunity to access to the right kind of information on agricultural inputs. They will also be given the opportunity of laearning and sharing best practices on appropriate technologies (for example, improved drought-tolerant seeds, and integrated pest management). Local inputs dealers will equally be involved to source women-friendly means of production and technologies. The project’s focus on cooperatives and women farmer groups structured around school meals programmes can create a physical space where women can build their confidence to learn and adopt new technologies, as well as gain negotiation and decision-making skills. Equally important, the cooperative activities will enable women farmers to have a new source of income independently from the household’s resources. Other areas where the project can improve the adaptive capacities of women and men is making weather and agriculture and market information readily available to both. The project will ensure wide and inclusive dissemination of information on cropping calendars, food prices, insurance, and micro-credit products etc.
C1. Increased dissemination of community-based risk preparedness measures and use of climate information services and insurance products (risk preparedness and risk transfer approach to address knowledge, regulatory and institutional barriers)
The component will implement community-based adaptation measures to increase the resilience of rural communities and restore the capacity of communal lands to cope with climate change hazards. An estimated 70 villages will be targeted and further identification and validation of areas and activities will be completed during the development of the Funding Proposal and at project inception. Following community and stakeholder consultations, the preliminary criteria for selection of sites and activities included[2] [https://wfp.sharepoint.com/sites/GCFCotedIvoire/Shared%20Documents/General/Concept%20Note%20development/Concept%20Note%20&%20attachments/4.%20Fourth%20submission%20to%20the%20GCF%20(December%202021)/GCF%20SAP-concept-note_Cote%20d'Ivoire_WFP_Revised_November2021_final.docx#_ftn2]:
* Incidence of climate impacts, * Vulnerability and adaptive capacity of villagers * Indicators of food and water insecurity * Initiatives undertaken by WFP and/or other stakeholders * The extent of degradation of communal lands * Availablity of financial services * Support from rural advisory and technical extension services * Structure and functionality of FOs
Outcome 1. Smallholder communities are better informed and prepared to cope with climate change hazards and threats
This outcome will leverage the dissemination of adaptation measures through local development plans and the implementation of on-the-ground restoration measures to enchance climate-resilience of rural population. They will also increase their planning and decision-making and investment capacity to deal with climate change impacts through improved access to climate information services and insurance products.
· Activity 1.1 Integration of climate change adaptation and distaster risk reduction measures in local development plans.
The activity will mainstream adaptation in communal plans to reduce vulnerability through an integrated approach that will identify appropriate measures and resources availability
· Activity 1.2 Implementation of community-based adaptation/risk management measures in vulnerable villages.
This activity will promote improved water management and water use efficiency as well as enhancing and improving soil fertility, for example by training local women and supporting them in taking leadership roles in management committees. It will also support restoration of communal lands around the selected villages. Climate-smart soil and water conservation and management will be implemented through an integrated approach that will include crop rotation, fallow and intercropping, soil cover improvement (mulch and plant cover), tillage systems with minimum soil disturbance. Water conservation measures will also include rainwater harvesting and improved water storage. Climate-smart land restoration will include planting of forest and fruit trees, residue management and avoid slash and burn and forest clearance based on measures identified in the adapted development plans. Women will be specifically targeted, ensuring they have access to information and decision-making.
· Activity 1.3 Provide project beneficiaries with Index-based Insurance products to mitigate climate change impacts of climate change hazards
The activity will support the development of index insurance products as risk transfer mechanism for rural communities, focusing on smallholder producers, protecting productive assets and leveraging livelihoods diversification options implemented under activities 1.2, 2.2 and 2.3 against climate shocks. During Funding Proposal development, a feasibility assessment will be carried out to evaluate the conditions and requirements to establish and disseminate sustainable insurance products based on previous experiences in the country and taking into account WFP’s expertise with similar initiatives in West Africa. Based on the preliminary assessment and consultations, WFP will establish the micro-insurance scheme with selected FOs that would include also incentives for its adoption, such as capacity-building, climate information services and a subsided premium that will be phased out over the years.
· Activity 1.4: Scale up the access and use of reliable, tailored and timely climate information and weather forecasts
The activity will allow smallholder farmers and other end-users across the food value chain to improve the access to tailored information for community-based adaptive planning and decision-making. Climate information will be made available through SMS, bulletins, leaflets, radio broadcasting sources (depending on the most appropriate and preferred channel by women) to enhance awareness on climate variability and tackle projected impacts of extreme weather events and slow-onset events through weather forecasts. In particular, the information will be shared in a way that will be suitable for women (for example in case of illiteracy) and they will be capacitated in their understanding and dissemination across communities.
C2. Increased smallholders’ adoption of climate-resilient practices and technologies across the food value chains (risk reduction approach to address technical, knowledge and gender barriers)
This component focuses on increasing the adaptive capacity of small-scale producers belonging to Farmers’ Organizations through climate-awareness, capacity building and scaling up of adaptive technologies and approaches in households’ farmlands.
Outcome 2. Smallholder producers improve and diversify food production and reduce post-harvest losses.
Individual and groups of farmers will improve their productivity across the food value chain by implementing nature-based agricultural practices and technologies and from benefiting from technical assistance and climate information services and products developed under component 1.
· Activity 2.1: Awareness-raising, capacity-building and organizational empowerment of smallholder farmers with focus on women and youths
The activity will support the capacity development of smallholder producers via the realization of trainings (e.g. in-person courses, seminars, webinars, e-learning); exchanges (e.g. peer-to-peer field visits, conferences, workshops, sharing platforms, communities of practice); technical assistance (e.g. expert missions, backstopping) focused on the implementation and scaling up of climate-resilient measures in households’ farmlands. In addition, awareness-raising campaigns will be included to leverage sensitization to target households (farmers and vulnerable communities). This activity, conducted in partnership with MINADER/ANADER, will provide the enabling environment for the scaling up and dissemination of adaptive technologies and practices planned under the activities 2.2 and 2.3. Adaptive technologies and practices will be further assessed and described during the FP development stage with the intention to systematize successful experiences and lessons learnt under activity 3.3 (knowledge management)
· Activity 2.2: Dissemination of adaptive nature-based agricultural practices, technologies and approaches to increase and diversify staple food production and improve soil and water conservation
Adaptive practices identified during preliminary consultations and project prefeasibility phase include provision of quality seeds of drought-tolerant varieties, implementation of conservation agriculture and agro-ecology practices, agroforestry, biopesticides and compost artisanal production. The approach for scaling up and dissemination of climate-resilient technologies will include a combination of farmer field schools, model farms, demonstrative plots and peer-to-peer exchange visits supported by extension and rural advisory to farmers’ groups provided by ANADER and mostly run by women.
· Activity 2.3 Improve processing and storage capacity to reduce post-harvest losses due to climate shocks
This activity will improve the access of post-harvest processing and storage technologies in favor of smallholder producers and actors across the food value chain. Small-scale processing equipment will include mills for maize and rice and solar driers for vegetables whereas silos and bags will be provided for efficient storage.
C3. Smallholder FOs improve market access, set savings schemes and leverage partnerships to strengthen the financial support across the food value chains (prudent risk taking approach to address financial and gender barriers)
The component is supporting community and household-based ownership and sustainability of the adaptive measures through increased financial and market access and knowledge dissemination. Basically, the component ensures that climate-proofing investments implemented respectively by communities and farm households under components 1 and 2 are sustained and spread across the Poro Region.
Outcome 3. Smallholders improve the financial sustainability of their food production systems
Climate adaptation measures are disseminated and continued after the projects thanks to the improved access to saving and loans mechanisms and complementarities generated with other resilience initiatives and enhanced market alliances.
· Activity 3.1. Support FOs to develop business plans and community-based saving and loans mechanisms for climate-proofing investments
This activity will focus on improving the financial literacy of members of FOs, and support the development of climate-resilient business plans to ensure complementarity with other climate-resilient initiatives under design, for example, the IGREENFIN Funding Proposal that falls under the GCF Great Green Wall Umbrella Programme. The establishment of Village-based Saving and Loans Associations (VSLA) will be another critical element to protect and incentivize climate-proofing investments and provide seed money for the implementation of business plans, therefore enhancing financial eligibility and complementarities with the IGREENFIN FP under design. Few options to ensure viability of the FOs will be analyzed and selected for the business plans. The linkages with IGREENFIN will be one of these, given the ongoing joint discussions on the design of the IFAD and WFP’s projects to promote funding options to FOs. However, other sources of livelihoods will be included, such as improved incomes from local/national market sales and school canteens. These latter are sources of incomes already established by WFP and will be scaled out through improved market information and commercialization of targeted project crops, in particular off-season vegetables. Finally, the establishment of VSLA, already proved successful in Western Africa will allow better efficiencies across the food value chain through for example the purchase of adapted inputs, agricultural products and tools for short-cycle crops which is the case for the selected project crops (maize, rice and vegetables). The resources provided to the VSLA will derive from the contribution of members of FOs that will improve the sales of agricultural products through adaptive crop production and improved market linkages. This will also build from existing local saving mechanisms, such as village-based loans or shared funds subscribed by a group of beneficiaries for a certain duration (‘’tontines’’).
· Activity 3.2 Build farm to market alliances in particular between FOs and school canteens and local markets
This activity will strengthen the capacity of targeted women smallholder producers to sell farm products through various options including improved linkages with school canteens and local markets. Moreover, the activity will strengthen capacities of public and private structures involved in food product commercialization with support of technology and IT equipment.
WFP has already established a channel to disseminate of market information through radio broadcasting and enhance partnerships with FOs under the school feeding program implemented across the country. This activity will exploit the potential of the market information services by including all the FOs covered by the project, facilitating producer-buyers exchanges and promoting alliances across the selected food value chains (maize, rice and vegetables) with local suppliers and intermediaries
· Activity 3.3 Systematization of good practices and knowledge-sharing of adaptive solutions across food value chains
This activity will collect and systematize successful experiences and lessons learnt related to adaptive technologies and good practices that have been implemented under activities 1.2, 1.3, 2.2 and 2.3. The deliverable of this activity will be a technical compendium of adaptation measures that will be shared with stakeholders with the intention to expand the dissemination and institutionalize the practices into local and national policies and plans.
3. WFP has been involved in resilience building in the project identified regions over the past 5 years. Much has been learned about sociocultural context in which the project will be implemented. WFP starts with strong advocacy which usually involves the participation of existing sociocultural and administrative structures in place in these communities. Community leaders play a crucial role in the buy-in of WFP’s proposed model of linking women farmer groups to local school meals programmes as the ultimate reason for the support to the smallholders. Land donation is a very participatory process that comes with sufficient safeguards from within each beneficiary communities. There exist various products from the proposed project that will meet the needs of both men and women it is designed to deliver activities that are participatory and converging in nature. This means both men and women will participate in productive assets’ restoration and regeneration and protection. The project delivery mechanism, messaging, advocacy will put emphasis on community resilience rather than the welfare of selected groups.
4. The transformational potential of the project revolves around strengthening the adaptive capacity and empowering smallholder farmers, in particular women and youths, who represent about 90 percent of direct beneficiaries, to reduce their vulnerability to climate shocks and sustainably improve the resilience of food production systems. The transformational and incremental distinction of the project consists in streamlining gender-sensitive actions for climate empowerment in an integrated manner. The project mainstreams an integrated community-based risk management approach: Risk reduction, risk preparedness, risk transfer, risk retention and prudent risk-taking that builds upon the R4 Programme successfully implemented by WFP in other areas of the continent, including West Africa.
5. The innovative elements of this project consists in strengthening the technical and financial capacity of women smallholder producers in order to:
· Mainstream climate risk and adaptive management practices through climate and market information,
· Enhance awareness and knowledge and promote the dissemination of climate-proofing technologies across priority food value chains,
· Introduce index-based micro-insurance products and strengthen financial inclusion of farmers in Poro Region as a way to promote climate-smart investments and protect productive assets,
· Leverage effective organizational capacity and women empowerment,
· Promote linkages and complementarities with other GCF Great Green Wall Umbrella Programme Initiatives, for example the IGREENFIN FP under formulation by strengthening the capacity of FOs to become self-sustaining through the development of business plans, and
· Support the establishment of market alliances between FOs and private actors to ensure the sustainability of the activities after the project.
In addition, the project will support the application of national adaptation strategies and plans at community and household levels by mainstreaming and implementing climate-resilient measures such as soil and water conservation, micro-watershed land restoration, adapted and sustainable staple crop production as part of the integrated livelihoods risk reduction strategy. Eventually, FOs in particular women and youths associations will be able to increase and diversify food supply to school feeding programmes and local markets through enhanced production, improved processing and storage, and better access to climate, financial and market services which will ensure viability and sustainaibility of project interventions.
Upon request from the Government of Côte d´Ivoire, WFP will be the Accredited Entity (AE) responsible for the oversight, reporting and monitoring of project activities and one of the Executing Entities (EE). Present in Côte d’Ivoire since 1969, WFP has been providing support according to the national development priorities. WFP’s operations consist on developing interventions to improve food security and livelihoods’ resilience, reduce malnutrition, enhance education and enhance gender equality. The project is aligned and contributes to the Strategic Outcome 4 of WFP’s 2019-2023 Country Strategic Plan: “Enhance food systems to be more sustainable and resilient”. Upon the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, WFP has introduced protective measures in its operations in line with Government´s guidelines[3] [https://wfp.sharepoint.com/sites/GCFCotedIvoire/Shared%20Documents/General/Concept%20Note%20development/Concept%20Note%20&%20attachments/4.%20Fourth%20submission%20to%20the%20GCF%20(December%202021)/GCF%20SAP-concept-note_Cote%20d'Ivoire_WFP_Revised_November2021_final.docx#_ftn3].
6. The Government of Côte d´Ivoire will act as Executing Entity (EE) through the MINADER. The National Agency for Rural Development Assistance (ANADER) as the operational Extension and Rural Advisory structure of MINADER will be tasked for the capacity-building, organizational empowerment and technical assistance. The Interprofessional Fund for Agricultural Research and Advisory (FIRCA), which is part of MINADER, will support the project financial management.
7. MINADER and WFP will be responsible for the day-to-day project execution ensuring that the objectives and outcomes are efficiently delivered on time. Given its mandate on climate change and its function as NDA for the GCF, the MINEDD will be responsible for ensuring alignment with national climate change adaptation priorities, for coordinating and drawing together the different ministries and national counterparts linked to project implementation, and for providing an advisory and monitoring role to WFP across the implementation of the project. The MINADER will be the sectoral counterpart institution tasked for the provision of technical assistance, knowledge dissemination, coordination and liaison with project beneficiaries to support ownership and sustainability of the interventions. The MINEDD will chair the Project Steering Committee (PSC) and assist in monitoring the achievement of the expected outputs. The MINADER will be the vice-chair of the PSC and be responsible for technical delivery, institutional ownership and sustainability of the interventions in alignment with the IGREENFIN project The Ministry of Education, Ministry of Solidarity and Promotion of Women, will contribute to the implementation of the project for gender actions for climate-empowerment and capacity-building activities. The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) will support the systematization and enabling environment for the dissemination of good adaptation practices. Other operational partners that have been pre-identified during the pre- feasibility assessment are: SODEXAM for climate-related information, microfinance institutions and mobile money platforms for insurance and financial services and Bureau de Vente aux Producteurs for market information services. As the project will start, the operational partners will be confirmed to better take into consideration the possible evolution of the context in Poro region and at national level.
8. The Project Management Unit will be tasked for the day-to-day monitoring activities including baseline data collection, field surveys, consultations with beneficiaries, preparation and follow-up of the annual work plan and budget, and dissemination of lessons learnt and successful experiences. The Project Steering Committee will meet twice a year to monitor achievement of project milestones and ensure that objectives are being accomplished.

9. Financial Risks:
· Financial services providers see smallholder farmers as high-risk investments (medium) in agricultural activities. Mitigation: The project will work with farmers’ organizations that will be supported and empowered through the project implementation. Financial providers will be selected during project pre-feasibility on the basis of their successful experiences in the Poro Region with producer’s organizations. In addition, village savings and loans groups will be the basis for financial inclusion and financial risk management at community level.
· Financial sustainability of climate-proofed investments (high). Mitigation: Organizations will develop climate-smart business plans, get access to savings and loans and complementarities with other climate-resilience initiatives.
· Basis risk challenges with the index-based Insurance product (medium). Mitigation: WFP will work with expert providers and in-house specialists to minimize such risk during product development and ensure indexes are adequately set and regularly updated. Crowd sourcing technology or area yield indices (based on crop cuts experiments) are 2 ways of lowering basis risk.
· Coverage and payment of insurance premiums (medium). Mitigation: The project will establish 2 mechanisms to address this risk: 1) savings and loans associations to protect protective assets and incentivize climate-proofing investments, and 2) improved yields and farmer household’s revenues expected from the implementation of adaptive technologies will be able to cover insurance premiums
10. Information gaps Risks:
Farmers do not have access or use climate information and weather forecasts provided by the project to adequately plan farm works and calendars (medium): Government and donor-funded initiative support the appropriate functioning of early warning system/hydromet network across the country. The project will catalyze the linkages between the information available and the dissemination to final users and build technical capacity for sustained use of climate information in farm management decision-making.
11. Operational Risks:
· Land tenure rights and conflicts linked to site interventions including transhumance (medium): the Project will conduct, prior to any site intervention, a community-based social and environmental screening. Also, the project will conduct a participatory planning exercise of the priority adaptive measures and mitigation options to avoid community conflicts over land tenure rights between farmers and transhumant herders. The community and municipal development plans will be amended to integrate adaptive measures through a participatory approach that will include the key stakeholders including community leaders, herders, and landowners. The ownership and management of productive assets, in particular land and water resources, will be defined at community level and monitored through the project implementation. Project activities, for example climate-smart land restoration, rehabilitation of storing facilities, soil conservation structures, etc. will be conditional to the allocation and contribution of community members (including both herders and farmers) and monitored by project team and community leaders. Women will be prioritized based on the gender analysis and action plan to reduce side-effects related to gender-based violence and women discrimination.
· Communities reluctant to adopt climate-resilient agriculture practices (low): Activities and approaches that will be utilized for the adoption and dissemination of climate-resilient agriculture practices and technologies in food production systems will include awareness-raising, trainings, peer-to-peer experience sharing, climate-resilient model farms and farmer field schools, access to microcredits and insurance for the uptake of climate-proofing investments.
· Insecurity due to political instability and terrorism (medium): The project will develop security and safety operation guidelines for personnel and partners. Likelihood of terrorist attacks in the project area is low.
· Limited operationality due to the COVID-19 pandemic public health restrictions (medium): It is highly likely that by the project start date, the pandemic could be under control. However, the project will closely monitor its evolution in close coordination with health authorities; all precautionary measures will be adopted to prevent the spread of the disease and mitigate the risk of low operationality in the area.
